title: start with the person in the mirror
hook: start with the person in the mirror
tomorrow: do something for someone with no receipt

segments.voice: Yesterday: the golden rule, your own heart as a map of someone else's. Today, the one person the map tends to leave out.

A friend burns the dinner. Misses a deadline. Says the wrong thing at the wrong moment. What comes out of your mouth? Usually something like: hey, it happens, you're tired, it's fine. Now flip it. You burn the dinner. What does the voice inside say then? Sometimes it's a voice nobody would be allowed to use on a friend. Idiot. Of course you did. Typical. One old tradition insists kindness starts with the person in the mirror.
screen: `WHAT YOU SAY TO A FRIEND.` → `WHAT YOU SAY TO YOURSELF.` → `START WITH THE MIRROR.`

segments.voice: In the early Buddhist teachings there's a word, metta. It's usually translated loving-kindness, but it comes from the Pali word for friend. Metta is friendliness: wanting good for someone the way a friend does. One short Buddhist discourse describes it with a picture: the way a mother would protect her only child with her own life, a person can grow a heart like that toward every living being. Here's the surprise. The Buddhist teacher Buddhaghosa wrote a long guide to meditation, and when he explains how to practice metta, he says not to start with everyone. Start with yourself. Wish yourself well first, with phrases like may I be happy, may I be free from trouble. Then extend it outward: to someone dear, to someone neutral, and eventually to someone difficult. His reasoning is plain. You know from the inside that you want to be happy. That makes you the example: everyone else wants the same. Remember yesterday's line from the Hebrew Bible: "love thy neighbour as thyself." Those last two words carry a quiet assumption: that there's some care for yourself to measure by. Modern research points somewhere similar. The psychologist Kristin Neff studies self-compassion: treating your own failures the way you'd treat a friend's. A common worry is that being kind to yourself will make you lazy. In one set of studies, people nudged to be gentler about a mistake were more willing to own it, and put more effort into doing better. Kindness isn't a reward for getting it right. It's where you start.
screen: `METTA: THE FRIEND WORD.` · `START WITH YOURSELF, THEN OUTWARD.` · `AS THYSELF.` · `GENTLE WITH MISTAKES, MORE LIKELY TO TRY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. The bell gives you about seventy-five seconds. Sit, and let the breath settle. Then picture yourself the way a good friend might see you right now: tired, trying, doing your best with the day you've had. On each breath out, say quietly inside: may I be at ease. If it feels strange or even a little silly, that's normal. Say it anyway.
Kindness. Wanting good for someone the way a friend does, starting with the one in the mirror. Sixteenth word.
Your line: may I be at ease. It's the sentence you'd give a friend, turned around. Day sixteen.

screen: `DAY 16 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: DO SOMETHING FOR SOMEONE WITH NO RECEIPT.`

howItsDone: In Buddhist loving-kindness (metta) meditation, practitioners often begin by silently wishing themselves well with a few short phrases, then extend the same wishes to a friend, a stranger, a difficult person and finally all beings.

original.note: Pali, from the Buddhist tradition: friendliness, loving-kindness. It comes from mitta, friend (Sanskrit maitrī).

trapdoor: what you thought: being nice to other people.
what it means: wanting good for someone the way a friend does, starting with yourself.
what a scholar hears: mettā, from mitta, friend, as the Visuddhimagga itself explains it; Buddhaghosa begins the practice with oneself, as the example, before extending it outward.

sources.ref: Visuddhimagga IX (development of loving-kindness, beginning with oneself)
Kristin Neff, research on self-compassion (e.g. Neff 2003; Breines & Chen 2012)

notes: Mettā from mitta (friend): standard etymology, and the Visuddhimagga (IX.93) gives it itself; confirm.
Metta Sutta's mother-and-only-child image is paraphrased (Sutta Nipata 149).
Visuddhimagga IX: Buddhaghosa says to develop loving-kindness first toward oneself, as the example, then a dear person, a neutral person, a hostile person.
The Leviticus observation ('as thyself' assumes some care for oneself) is framed as a reader's observation, not a Jewish teaching; a Jewish Keeper may want to review.
Self-compassion findings (e.g. Breines & Chen 2012: self-compassion increased motivation to improve after failure) are summarized loosely as 'one set of studies'; confirm.
Practice words 'may I be at ease' are a traditional-style metta phrase given as the day's carry, not a new prayer.
